#QIResearch
BLS Employment Situation In December 2025 And Reading Past the Noise
The unemployment rate is just unemployed divided by the labor force. In December, the number of unemployed fell by 278k, while employment rose 232k and the labor force slipped 46k. That combination mechanically pushes the rate down (from 4.5% to 4.4%). The “improvement” is mostly a numerator story (fewer counted as unemployed) with a small assist from the denominator (a slightly smaller labor force).  
Then read the footnotes (where the real story lives)
Two things matter here if you’re being skeptical…
•   Seasonal adjustment got revised. BLS updated seasonal factors and revised household survey history. Notably, November’s unemployment rate was revised down (4.6 to 4.5). So part of the drop people see is revision plus seasonality, not some dramatic new shift in December.
•   This is household survey territory, it’s noisy. BLS basically tells you this in the technical note: the monthly change in the unemployment rate has a confidence interval on the order of ±0.2 percentage point. A 0.1 move is not a clean signal. It’s a watch it, not a declare it. 
If You’re Hunting Recession Fingerprints, Don’t Stare At U-3
The recessionary tells in this report aren’t the headline rate, they’re the quality and persistence underneath it…
•   Underemployment is elevated. People working part time for economic reasons are 5.3M, and that’s up 980k over the year. That’s employers and workers meeting each other at the margin, not in confident full time hiring.  
•   Hidden slack is growing. People not in the labor force who currently want a job are 6.2M, up 684k over the year. That’s the quiet way labor markets weaken: more people want work, but they’re not counted in U-3 because they aren’t “actively”searching in the last 4 weeks.  
•   Long term unemployment is creeping. Long term unemployed are 1.9M, up 397k over the year, and they’re 26% of all unemployed. That’s a classic late cycle deterioration: hiring slows, and unemployment becomes stickier.  
•   Broader measures still look worse than a year ago. Even though they improved a bit in December, U-6 is 8.4% (vs 7.6% a year ago), and U-4/U-5 follow the same better this month, worse over the year pattern.  
The Payroll Survey Is Waving A Bigger Red Flag Than The Unemployment Rate
Payrolls were +50k and BLS basically says you can’t hang your hat on that month to month: the confidence band for monthly payroll change is large enough that +50k can still be no change statistically.  
The more important tells…
•   The 3 month average payroll change is negative (about ‑22k). That’s stall speed.
•   Revisions went the wrong way. October and November were revised down (combined ‑76k). In turning points, revisions often betray the initial optimism.  
•   Sector mix looks defensive. Gains are concentrated in food services, health care, social assistance while retail trade lost 25k and areas like transport and warehousing and temp help are weak. That’s households still spending, but the goods and credit cycle is tightening.  
•Hours are slipping. The workweek edged down, and the aggregate hours index fell. In real downturns, employers usually cut hours first, then heads. This is the early part of that movie.  
The Outlier I’d Circle In Red Ink 
Federal government employment down 277k since January (‑9.2%) is a huge swing and the report explicitly notes that people on paid leave or ongoing severance can still be counted as employed in the establishment survey. Essentially some labor market pain can get time shifted in how it shows up.

title: This Chart Explains Why the Economy Feels Off
content:
This Chart Explains Why the Economy Feels Off
This chart isn’t about a bad quarter or a quirky data revision. It’s showing a long, structural shift. For decades after World War II, workers reliably took a little over 60% of the economic pie. That wasn’t accidental. It reflected strong unions, tighter regulation, limited globalization, and a system that funneled productivity gains back into wages.
That floor started cracking in the 1980s. It never truly came back. And over the last twenty years especially after 2000 the decline stopped being cyclical and became structural. The latest reading just makes that impossible to ignore. Labor’s share isn’t low relative to the past few years. It’s low relative to modern U.S. history.
This isn’t about workers suddenly becoming less productive. Productivity has actually been decent. The problem is that productivity gains aren’t flowing to paychecks. They’re flowing to margins.
Why This Keeps Happening
The story underneath is bargaining power. Globalization, automation, weaker labor institutions, and rising market concentration all tilt leverage away from workers. Large, dominant firms can scale without hiring much labor. Care and service jobs add headcount, but they don’t reset wage power across the economy. So employment can grow while labor’s slice shrinks.
Policy matters here too, but not always in the way people think. Asset supportive policies helped stabilize the economy after crises, but they also boosted capital values much faster than wages. That cushions downturns without fixing distribution. Over time, that gap compounds.
You can see it in the data around this chart with weak hiring momentum, more people working multiple jobs, slower real wage growth, and profits holding up fine. That combination almost guarantees downward pressure on labor share.
What It Means For The Economy
A falling labor share doesn’t just show up as inequality. It changes how the economy behaves. When income shifts toward capital, spending becomes more fragile. Growth leans harder on credit, fiscal support, or asset wealth effects. Things can look stable on the surface while feeling tight underneath.
Markets often like this setup at first. Lower labor costs support margins. Inflation stays contained. Stocks do fine. But over time, revenue growth gets harder if workers can’t keep spending. And eventually the imbalance shows up somewhere else…politically, socially, or financially.
My View
This chart isn’t a warning about tomorrow. It’s a diagnosis of the system we’re already in. Productivity is still there. Growth is still possible. But the link between economic gains and worker pay has weakened to a degree we haven’t seen before.
That doesn’t break the economy overnight. It slowly changes its character. And history says that when labor’s share gets this low, it stops being just an economic statistic and starts becoming a macro force of its own.

title: An underemployment rate of 41.8% for recent colleg...
content:
An underemployment rate of 41.8% for recent college graduates means more than four in ten are either unemployed or working jobs that don’t really match their education. For context, the dot com bust peaked around 38.5% in late 2002, after tech hiring froze. During COVID, the rate briefly jumped to about 43.2%, but that was a sudden shutdown followed by a rapid reopening. The Great Financial Crisis was worse, underemployment for recent grads ultimately pushed close to 50%, but crucially, that peak didn’t arrive until years after the recession officially began.
What’s unsettling now is the timing. We’re already above dot com levels and not far from COVID peaks, without an officially declared recession and while headline unemployment still looks fine 
🧐
🤔
Historically, that only happens when hiring has quietly broken first. Firms don’t start by firing experienced workers; they stop hiring, freeze entry level roles, and downgrade jobs. New grads feel it immediately. Either hiring rebounds hard from here, or this is doing what it’s usually done in the past, flagging a labor market that’s weaker than it looks before the broader data catches up.
Underemployment rate for recent college graduates rose to 41.8%, per New York Fed.

title: 2025 Wasn’t the Downturn. It Was the Setup
content:
2025 Wasn’t the Downturn. It Was the Setup
2025 really does stand out as the worst year for hiring since 2020, and what matters is how it earned that distinction. Unlike COVID in 2020, there was no sudden shutdown or snapback. Unlike the Great Financial Crisis of 2008–2009, there wasn’t a system-wide credit seizure or mass layoffs. And unlike the dot com bust of 2001–2002, the damage wasn’t confined to one overheated sector. Instead, hiring quietly dried up across much of the economy while firms held on to existing workers, masking deterioration behind superficially stable headlines…weak job growth, downward revisions, stalled quits, and longer job searches.
That’s why 2025 was a different kind of bad. It looked like a slow motion stall, a low hire, low fire environment where companies protected margins, paused expansion, and stopped creating new opportunities. The stress showed up where it always does first in things like rising credit card delinquencies concentrated among lower income households, mounting auto and student loan strain, record office distress, higher bankruptcies, and more people working multiple jobs just to keep up. Historically, this is how labor markets weaken before they break. Entry level roles disappear first, underemployment rises, and confidence erodes long before unemployment spikes. If 2001–2002 was about excess, 2008–2009 was about systemic failure, and 2020 was about a policy shock, then 2025 was about quiet accumulation…demand slowing, rates staying restrictive, and businesses trying to do more with fewer people. And this wasn’t a closing chapter; it was a setup. The forces that defined 2025 didn’t resolve, which means the real test of this cycle carries straight into 2026.
2025 the worst year for hiring since 2020, when pandemic shut down the U.S. economy.

title: The record holiday spend is real, but it’s also de...
content:
The record holiday spend is real, but it’s also deceiving, because it mixes together a bunch of things that don’t mean the consumer is strong. 
First, the 6.8% YoY growth looks solid until you remember that prices have been higher for years, and this pace is actually slower than 2024’s growth. So a record in dollars can just be the same basket of goods getting rung up at higher prices, plus a little volume, not some booming surge in real demand. It’s a nominal record, not automatically a real one.
Second, the season was engineered to look strong. The fact there were 25 days over $4B and Cyber Week up 7.7% tells you retailers successfully stretched the calendar and pulled demand forward with constant promos. When deals start earlier every year, you get more big spend days, but that’s partly just timing and marketing, not household confidence. Even the spike in mobile share 56.4% of online purchases, 66.5% on Christmas Day is less people are rich and more shopping is frictionless now. One click spending is not the same thing as discretionary breathing room.
Third, the red flag is buried in the fine print: BNPL hit $20B, up 9.8% growing faster than total sales. That’s the tell. When the financing method is outgrowing the spending itself, you’re not watching abundance, you’re watching affordability stress. People didn’t just spend; they borrowed to spend. That’s how you get a strong holiday print and a weaker Q1.
And lastly, the +693% jump in generative AI driven shopping traffic sounds futuristic, but it also fits the same story where consumers are hunting for deals harder than ever, and retailers are getting better at capturing that behavior. It’s optimization, not necessarily prosperity. Put it all together and the record spending starts to look less like a healthy consumer and more like a consumer being kept afloat by discounts, convenience, and credit which can absolutely produce a great holiday season… right before the hangover shows up in delinquencies and pullbacks.
BREAKING: US holiday online shopping surged +6.8% YoY, to a record $257.8 billion, between November 1st to December 31st, 2025.
This marks at least the 6th consecutive annual increase. 
There were 25 days where daily spending exceeded $4 billion, up from 18 days in 2024.
Cyber Week sales alone jumped +7.7% YoY, to a record $44.2 billion, with Cyber Monday sales jumping +7.1% YoY, to $14.3 billion.
Mobile shopping accounted for 56.4% of all online transactions, reaching 66.5% on Christmas Day.
Furthermore, "Buy Now Pay Later" spending rose +9.8% YoY, to $20.0 billion for the first time.
Meanwhile, traffic to retail sites from generative AI tools surged +693% YoY as consumers used AI shopping assistants to find deals.
Consumers borrowed and spent at a record pace this holiday season. 
- 
The Kobeissi Letter

title: “The United States will take Greenland the ‘easy w...
content:
“The United States will take Greenland the ‘easy way’ or the ‘hard way.’”
“If we don’t do it, Russia or China will.”
Trump just said the quiet part out loud and the bluntness is the point….
Greenland is not a place you want for comfort; it is a place you need for foresight. It stands where the world thins and distance collapses, where the curve of the Earth bends strategy toward those who arrive first. In the high north, power moves without noise. The ice opens, the routes lengthen, the warning times shorten. Geography, long ignored, returns with authority.
From that frozen spine, the sky speaks sooner. Radar reaches farther. Missiles are seen earlier. Submarines lose silence. This is why listening posts live there, why earl warning systems cling to that latitude, why airfields carved into ice matter more than capitals filled with speeches. Greenland is not land, it is time. And time is the rarest weapon.
Beneath the surface lies the materials of the next century. Rare earths, critical minerals, energy locked under cold pressure. The modern world runs on what it extracts from hard places, not what it promises in soft rooms. Whoever controls supply controls continuity. Whoever controls continuity survives disruption.
Others understand this instinctively. Russia spreads itself along the Arctic rim, stitching bases into the cold. China names itself near to a place it cannot touch without leverage, investing patiently, thinking in decades. Neither sees Greenland as remote. Both see it as inevitable.
So the language hardens. Not because conquest is desired, but because delay is dangerous. Great powers fall when they hesitate at thresholds. Greenland is such a threshold. A gate between oceans, continents, and futures.
To stand there is not to threaten the world. It is to refuse blindness. And in an age where the future moves faster than diplomacy, blindness is the one mistake no empire survives.

title: This is a year to date accumulation of announced l...
content:
This is a year to date accumulation of announced layoffs. By the end of 2025, companies had flagged just over 1.2 million job cuts, which puts the year in rare territory outside of crisis moments. That’s why the 2025 line sits up near the Great Financial Crisis years. It reflects a broad shift in behavior..protect margins, cut headcount, slow hiring and conserve cash.
What makes this different from a normal tech cycle reset is how wide it spread. Government cuts hit early and hard, tech followed, but then you see retail, warehousing, and services join in. At the same time, planned hiring quietly fell to levels we usually only see after growth has already cracked. That’s the part markets often miss..layoffs matter, but the absence of new hiring matters more.
Excluding COVID, What Does History Say Comes Next?
If you strip out 2020 and look at prior years that hit this kind of annual layoff scale 2001, 2002–03, 2008–09 the economy was either in recession or stuck in a post recession labor slump. There aren’t many clean counterexamples where layoffs ran this hot and the economy just shrugged it off.
Put simply..
•Historically, there’s about a 60% chance this level of layoffs coincides with an official recession.
•If you widen the lens to include recessionary conditions..weak growth, soft labor demand, rising slack..the odds climb closer to 75–80%.
That doesn’t mean collapse is guaranteed. It does mean the labor market is no longer a buffer and it’s becoming a transmission channel.
My View
This chart is signaling late cycle behavior with a strong track record. Companies don’t announce layoffs at this scale because they’re feeling confident about demand 6 months out. They do it because uncertainty is rising and flexibility matters more than expansion.
When layoffs stack up and hiring dries up, history says the economy usually bends next. Whether it snaps or just sags depends on what breaks first..credit, consumers, or confidence.

title: The BLS Productivity and Costs Report Shows an Eco...
content:
The BLS Productivity and Costs Report Shows an Economy Leaning on Discipline, Not Growth
The headline is easy to like. Labor productivity jumped 4.9% in Q3 2025, one of the stronger quarterly prints in years. Output rose 5.4%, while hours worked barely moved, up just 0.5%. On paper, that looks like the economy getting more efficient, more goods and services produced without needing a lot more labor.  
But productivity is a ratio, not a feeling. It’s output divided by hours. So the only real question is which side of that equation is doing the heavy lifting.
Output Is Carrying the Headline For Now
This quarter, the productivity gain is mostly output driven, not the classic recession pattern where productivity rises because hours collapse. That matters. In broad nonfarm business, hours are still rising slightly, and unit labor costs actually fell 1.9% in the quarter as productivity outran wage growth.  
That’s the part the all clear crowd focuses on…
•   Output is growing.
•   Costs per unit of labor are easing.
•   Inflation pressure looks more contained.
On its own, that’s not recessionary.
Where The Cracks Start To Show
The tension shows up when you look beneath the aggregate.
In manufacturing, productivity rose 3.3%, but only because hours worked fell 0.7%. Durable goods are even starker: output up 3.0%, hours down 1.7%.  
That’s a very different posture. Firms aren’t scaling up labor to meet demand; they’re squeezing more out of fewer hours. That’s usually a sign of caution, not confidence.
At the same time, manufacturing unit labor costs are still rising year over year, even with better productivity. That means margins are under pressure, not expanding cleanly.  
The Profit Check Most People Miss
The most telling line in the report isn’t productivity at all, it’s profits.
In the nonfinancial corporate sector, unit profits jumped 6.6% in Q3, but over the last four quarters they’re actually down 0.3%.  
That combination matters. When profits flatten or slip over a full year while costs remain sticky, companies don’t respond with optimism. They respond with restraint with fewer hours, slower hiring, delayed investment. That’s often how labor markets weaken quietly before layoffs show up in force.
Why the Economy Hasn’t Tipped Over…Yet
Taken together, this report doesn’t scream downturn. The productivity surge isn’t being driven by mass job cuts, and output is still growing. But it does show an economy leaning more on discipline than expansion.
The outliers to watch aren’t the headline numbers. They’re the subtle ones…
•   Hours falling in cyclical sectors.
•   Manufacturing costs that won’t come down easily.
•   Profits that look fine quarter to quarter, but stall over the year.
If future productivity gains start coming from hours falling faster than output, rather than output accelerating, the story changes quickly. That’s when productivity stops being a strength and starts being a warning.
For now, this looks like an economy still moving forward but doing so carefully, and with less margin for error than the headline suggests.

title: Caracas is a thin, fragile market, and when a shoc...
content:
Caracas is a thin, fragile market, and when a shock headline hits especially one that changes the political endgame prices don’t glide higher, they jump. Buyers hit whatever was for sale, sellers step back, and the index gaps because there’s no depth to absorb the flow. In markets like this, price moves don’t reflect consensus, they reflect scarcity.
Why This Happens After a Political Shock
The capture of Maduro isn’t being priced as a policy outcome yet, it’s being priced as optionality. Sanctions relief, reopening oil exports, foreign capital returning… none of that has happened, but the probability just went from near zero to “maybe.” When that tail risk shifts, distressed assets reprice fast.
Layer on local behavior and it accelerates. In unstable regimes, people don’t rush into cash they rush out of it. Stocks, even broken ones, become a hedge against currency risk and political chaos. Add a few momentum traders and exiles trying to front run a reopening, and in a market this illiquid, you get a vertical move.
The Broader Pattern (and the Risk)
This isn’t unique. You saw the same dynamics in post Soviet Russia in the 1990s, and again during Argentina’s debt restructurings. Emerging markets can deliver eye watering upside when the story flips but they do it with just as much speed on the way down. Thin liquidity cuts both ways.
The real test isn’t the first candle, it’s what comes next. Does volume follow? Do prices hold once the initial euphoria fades? And does reality of sanctions policy, oil flows, political stability confirm the narrative?
If you’re watching this in real time, oil futures and sanction headlines matter more than technicals right now. That’s where confirmation or disappointment will show up first.

title: The cash numbers  $10k, $100k, whatever the range ...
content:
The cash numbers  $10k, $100k, whatever the range is are almost a decoy. The point is to speak over Denmark and talk directly to Greenlanders, as if sovereignty were negotiable the way a contract is negotiable: here is a better deal; here is a different future; choose it. That’s not a real estate pitch. It’s an attempt to rewrite the political frame from territory to terms.
And once you do that, everything else follows. You make the island’s relationship with Copenhagen feel conditional, transactional, outdated. You turn independence from an abstract dream into a concrete balance sheet: more money, more jobs, more infrastructure, more leverage. In practice, that means you’re trying to manufacture consent the way markets do, by shifting incentives until the “rational” choice becomes the one you want.
The macro logic is obvious if you zoom out. Greenland is not just ice; it’s position. It sits on the Arctic geometry where shipping routes open, where submarines move, where early warning matters, where space and missile defense live. It’s also inputs like rare earth potential, resource optionality, future supply chain control. You don’t need to extract every ounce for it to matter; you need to deny clean access to rivals and anchor the region to your security perimeter.
So what he’s trying to do is less conquest than preemption. Preempt Russia’s reach across the Arctic, preempt China’s slow burn influence through capital and infrastructure, preempt Europe’s assumption that this space remains theirs by default. A check written to citizens is a way of saying: we’re not negotiating with states alone anymore; we’re negotiating with populations.
And that’s why it’s so provocative. Because it asks a quiet, destabilizing question: what is a country, if not a set of people who can be offered a different deal? Denmark hears it as intrusion. Greenland hears it as possibility. Washington hears it as strategy.
It’s the modern empire move…not flags first …incentives first. Then the map changes on its own.

title: There’s a quiet moment in this chart where you rea...
content:
There’s a quiet moment in this chart where you realize it isn’t really about gas.
It’s about who gets to decide what energy security means when the pipes are gone and the ocean is the pipeline.
If these figures are right, the U.S. didn’t just have a strong year, it crossed into something structural: +25% in 2025 to a record 116 million tons, the first country to clear 100 million tons in a single year, with December hitting 11.5 million tons on its own. And the punchline isn’t just volume, it’s share: 25% of global LNG exports, roughly 20 million tons ahead of the next biggest exporters (Qatar and Australia), with another 20 million tons potentially coming online in 2026 as new capacity ramps.
This is the U.S. turning a commodity into a lever.
Because LNG isn’t like oil. Oil is liquid and global by nature. LNG is a chain of choke points…liquefaction trains, shipping slots, regas terminals, contracts, insurance, politics. The U.S. gaining scale here means it’s not just selling energy. It’s quietly shaping the marginal price of Europe’s winter, the risk premium on Russia, the bargaining power of Qatar, and the industrial cost curve that every export economy eventually has to answer to.
And the timing matters. Post Nord Stream
🧐
🤔
 Europe’s energy reality got rewritten in one season…pipeline dependence became a vulnerability, and LNG became the bridge. The U.S. stepped into that gap not with speeches, but with cargoes and cargoes have a way of becoming policy without ever calling themselves policy.
This is geopolitical influence with a shipping manifest. Not empire in the old flag and forts sense…empire as optionality. The ability to stabilize allies, squeeze adversaries, and quietly price in your own strategic priorities through long term contracts and spot cargoes.
The second order effect is where it gets real. Once a region builds its energy system around your supply, it doesn’t just buy molecules it buys your time, your trade routes, your insurance markets, your sanctions architecture, your dollar plumbing. Even the argument about diversification starts to sound like a different kind of dependence.
So yes, it’s a record. But it’s also a change in the map.
Because when one country becomes the swing supplier of the thing that keeps lights on and factories running, the world doesn’t just heat homes differently.
It negotiates differently.
US dominance in global LNG exports is growing:
US LNG exports surged +25% in 2025, to a record 116 million tons.
This makes the US the first country in history to export more than 100 million tons of LNG in a single year.
December exports alone hit an all-time high of 11.5 million tons, marking the 5th monthly record of 2025.
The US now represents ~25% of global LNG exports, nearly 20 million tons more than the next largest exporters, Qatar and Australia.
With new projects ramping up, US LNG exports could rise by another 20 million tons in 2026.
The shale revolution is redefining global energy dynamics.

title: US households are now sending an unusually large s...
content:
US households are now sending an unusually large share of their take home pay to debt. 
Total debt service is up to 30% of gross disposable national income.
That means if you add up all after tax income in the country and compare it to all the monthly payments on mortgages, credit cards, car loans, student loans, etc., about 30 cents of every dollar of income is going to debt payments. 
That is close to the highest level since right before the 2008 financial crisis.
Those payments break into two pieces. 
Around 10% of income is just interest, which is the cost of borrowing. 
Because interest rates have risen so much over the last few years, the same amount of debt now costs more to carry each month. 
The other ~18% is principal, which is the actual loan balances being paid down. 
That principal share is also at the highest level since at least 2008. 
On top of that, the total stock of household debt is at a record in dollar terms, roughly 18.6 trillion. 
So there is more debt than ever, and it is more expensive to service.
The key economic implication is about spending power. 
If about 1 out of every 3 dollars of take home pay is locked into mandatory debt payments, there is less money left for everything else, restaurants, travel, home improvements, services, even basic goods if budgets are tight. 
Debt service works like a silent tax on households. 
When this ratio climbs, sectors that depend on discretionary spending tend to feel it first, and overall consumer‑driven growth can slow.
There is also a financial health angle. 
High debt burdens make households more vulnerable to shocks. If someone loses a job or faces a medical bill and they are already using a large chunk of income on debt, it becomes harder to keep up.
That can translate into rising delinquencies and defaults on credit cards, auto loans and other forms of credit, which then nudges lenders to tighten standards. 
To be clear, this doesn’t automatically mean a repeat of 2008, but the message of the chart is that the cushion in household budgets is getting thinner.
That makes the economy more sensitive to any new negative shock because consumers have less room to absorb it.
The US household debt burden has almost never been this large:
US household total debt service is up to 30% of gross disposable national income, the highest since at least 2008.
This means the average American household is now spending nearly 1 out of every 3 Dollars they earn after taxes just to pay off debt.
This comes as household debt interest payments are up to ~10%, the highest in at least 18 years.
Furthermore, total US household debt surged +$197 billion in Q3 2025, to a record $18.6 trillion.
Meanwhile, principal amortization, or the portion of debt payments that goes toward paying down the actual loan balance, not interest, is up to ~18%, the highest since at least 2008.
The debt burden is squeezing consumer spending power.

title: AWS, Ripple, and the Quiet Work of Making Things H...
content:
AWS, Ripple, and the Quiet Work of Making Things Hold
This is not a story about checkout buttons or sudden adoption. It’s a story about plumbing and about what happens beneath the surface when a system grows large enough that “mostly works” is no longer good enough.
From what’s been reported, Amazon Web Services and Ripple are exploring the use of Amazon Bedrock to help sift through the XRP Ledger’s system logs, turning days of manual diagnosis into minutes. That’s not spectacle. That’s maintenance. And maintenance is where systems either mature or quietly fail.
For AWS, this is a clean, intelligible use case for Bedrock…AI applied to monitoring, reliability, incident response, the unglamorous work enterprises actually pay for. Once logs, workflows, and alerting live inside AWS’s orbit, they tend to stay there. This is how platforms entrench themselves, not with announcements, but with dependency.
For Ripple, the logic is just as plain. Faster detection and repair lowers the friction of running a global, distributed ledger. It shortens the distance between something going wrong and someone fixing it. That’s how a network moves from functional to trustworthy, especially when institutions are watching and the margin for error narrows.
And XRP itself? It remains where it has always been…the native asset that makes the ledger function with fees, liquidity, settlement. This doesn’t wire XRP into Amazon’s storefront, and it doesn’t need to. Infrastructure comes first. If the rails become more reliable, more use can follow. If they don’t, no narrative can save them.
There are hints this isn’t happening in isolation. Ripple’s appearance in AWS’s ecosystem, like re:Invent sessions focused on intelligent, always on operational systems fits this same arc. Everything else you’ll hear, especially the louder claims, should be treated gently until they appear in primary AWS or Ripple statements.
This is how real progress tends to arrive…quietly, through better tools, shorter outages, and systems learning how to watch themselves. Not a price catalyst. Not a promise. Just the slow, necessary work of making something sturdy enough to last.

title: A write down sounds tidy, clerical, as though some...
content:
A write down sounds tidy, clerical, as though someone merely dimmed a light in the books. But this one is heavier than that. GM’s $6 billion EV charge is the sound of momentum meeting resistance, of plans made in one mood colliding with a world that has quietly shifted its weight.
The Moment the Story Changed
For a while, the future arrived early. Subsidies smoothed the path, demand seemed willing, and the curve felt inevitable. Then the $7,500 credit vanished, interest rates stayed high, and buyers hesitated. Not dramatically just enough. And that just enough is always where things break. Contracts signed for speed suddenly looked like anchors. Suppliers built for volume that never quite came.
What the Write Down Really Is
This isn’t about abandoning electric vehicles. It’s about paying, now, to loosen commitments made too confidently, too soon. Much of the charge is real cash…settlements, cancellations, the cost of admitting that the ramp would be slower, more uneven, more political than the forecasts allowed. Ford’s larger write down nearby in time only sharpens the point: this isn’t one company blinking, it’s an industry resetting its tempo.
The Deeper Signal
GM is buying time, and flexibility, at a painful price. The technology isn’t the problem. The timeline was. EVs are still coming, but not as a clean, subsidized sprint. More like a long walk with pauses, reversals, and recalculations along the way. And in moments like this, the bravest move isn’t to push harder…it’s to stop, take the loss, and admit the road bends more than expected.

title: A Policy Pitch for a Cycle That’s Already Turning
content:
A Policy Pitch for a Cycle That’s Already Turning
It is offered as a neat exchange…two institutions, flush with cash, reach into the market, buy mortgage bonds, and the cost of shelter eases. A gesture of order, almost domestic in its calm. Two hundred billion becomes a number you can hold in your hand, and with it the suggestion that affordability, once misplaced, can be guided gently home again.
It sounds powerful because it feels direct. It gives the impression that the problem has been located, named, and addressed.
What the Market Actually Hears
But markets listen differently. Buying mortgage backed securities can narrow the spread, the extra margin lenders charge over Treasuries and that does matter at the edges. It is the same channel the Fed once used when it wanted housing to breathe more easily. Still, this is a subtle adjustment, measured in tens of basis points, not a sweeping turn of the wheel.
The deeper rate, the 10 year…moves to another rhythm entirely. It responds to growth slowing, to inflation expectations bending lower, to unemployment beginning to rise and households pulling back. When hiring softens and confidence thins, capital seeks safety. Yields fall not because they are pushed, but because they are drawn.
The Unspoken Sequence
This is the part that rarely makes the headline. If the economy cools, if layoffs spread quietly, if hours shrink before jobs do, if spending loses its urgency, the 10 year will come down on its own. Mortgage rates will follow, dragged by gravity rather than design. And when that happens, the story is ready made…rates fell because someone acted, not because the cycle turned.
In that sense, the announcement itself does work. It tightens spreads on expectation. It gives markets a reason to lean forward. Even a half!formed plan can function as a kind of persuasion.
The Weight Beneath the Floor
Yet Fannie and Freddie are not free hands moving cash across a table. They sit inside the long shadow of 2008, bound by conservatorship, regulation, and memory. Forcing scale into MBS would concentrate risk once more in the housing state machine, even as lower rates in a supply!starved market threaten to lift prices faster than incomes can follow.
Affordability, then, slips sideways. Payments ease, values rise, and the tension remains.
What I Keep Coming Back To
This feels less like a lever than a lens. A way to frame what may already be approaching. If unemployment rises and growth expectations fall, yields will come down regardless. The economy will do the heavy lifting. The policy, spoken early and confidently, will claim the result.
And that is the quiet brilliance of it…when the weather changes, it helps to already have a name for the storm and a story about who called it in.

title: This chart tracks how asset managers are positione...
content:
This chart tracks how asset managers are positioned in VIX futures, and right now it’s flashing something familiar…a very large bet that volatility stays low. In plain terms, a lot of money is leaning into the idea that markets will remain orderly, dips will be shallow, and any shocks will be managed. Historically, extremes like this don’t signal an immediate crash but they do tell you psychology has shifted toward comfort.
Why That Comfort Matters
Short volatility trades work best when nothing happens. The problem is that when everyone crowds into the same calm, the system becomes fragile. We’ve seen this before 2006–07, parts of 2017, and again heading into late 2018. Volatility stayed compressed…until it didn’t. When it turns, it tends to turn fast, because the unwind itself creates volatility.
Cause, Effect, And The Historical Rhyme
Importantly, a big VIX short isn’t a forecast of doom. Volatility backwardation or positioning extremes don’t guarantee a down market, and strong equity rallies have often followed periods of stress or dislocation. The signal here is narrower…markets are priced for stability at a time when macro uncertainty with rates, growth, geopolitics hasn’t actually gone away. That gap between calm pricing and noisy reality is where surprises come from.
My Take
This isn’t about predicting a crash. It’s about asymmetry. When volatility is heavily shorted, upside surprises are limited and downside shocks travel faster. The trade works…right up until the moment it doesn’t. And history says those moments tend to arrive when confidence feels least questioned.

title: Why Honduras Matters More Than It Looks in the Nic...
content:
Why Honduras Matters More Than It Looks in the Nicaragua Play
I still think the December 2, 2025 pardon of former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández matters most in the Nicaragua phase of what increasingly looks like a Donroe Doctrine sequencing. The logic isn’t ideological; it’s operational. Honduras borders Nicaragua, and in Central America, proximity is leverage.
What complicates and sharpens that leverage is what happened immediately after the pardon. Just days after Hernández was released from U.S. prison, Honduras’ Attorney General, Johel Antonio Zelaya, issued a domestic arrest warrant on December 9, 2025. These charges are separate from the U.S. drug case and center on fraud, money laundering, and the alleged diversion of more than $12 million in state funds tied to the Pandora corruption scandal. As of today, the warrant remains active, and Hernández is reportedly staying out of the country as a result. That timing matters. It preserves the pardon’s geopolitical signaling to Washington while keeping Hernández legally sidelined at home, an outcome that quietly stabilizes the transition without forcing an immediate reckoning.
The pardon itself helped reset Honduras political alignment at a sensitive moment. Nasry “Tito” Asfura’s November 30, 2025 election win, certified just before year end returned a pro U.S. government after a leftist interlude. That puts Honduras back in position as the frontline state for pressure on Daniel Ortega’s Nicaragua. Intelligence cooperation, border enforcement, migration control, and indirect support for opposition networks all become easier with a cooperative government next door. This fits the broader sequencing with Venezuela first, Nicaragua next, Cuba as the eventual capstone, with Mexico running in parallel.
It’s also important to be precise about who controls what right now. Asfura isn’t yet in office and Honduran inaugurations don’t happen until January 27 so the current left leaning Castro administration still controls the justice system and issued the warrant. Asfura has no formal authority to intervene at this stage, and he’s made no public move to revoke or enforce it. That ambiguity is useful. It allows the incoming government to distance itself from Hernández’s baggage while benefiting from the political realignment his pardon helped unlock. If the warrant quietly stands after inauguration, it can be framed as respect for judicial independence or anti corruption credibility, rather than political retaliation though any such interpretation remains speculative.
There’s a colder, transactional message running through all of this. The pardon signals to regional elites that alignment still buys protection at the strategic level, even if legal accountability doesn’t disappear entirely. In Nicaragua’s case, that signal can be more powerful than sanctions alone. It encourages hesitation, defections, and recalculation inside Ortega’s circle without requiring overt U.S. escalation. As WOLA has noted, this reflects a broader shift in U.S. policy with a willingness to tolerate imperfections in friendly regimes to secure hemispheric control and block rival influence.
Taken together, the sequence turns Honduras into a disciplined pressure point rather than a liability. Hernández is neutralized without destabilizing the transition, Asfura inherits a cooperative relationship with Washington, and Nicaragua faces a tighter perimeter just as pressure ramps up through tools like early 2026 tariffs. There’s always a risk of backlash, but structurally, this looks less like inconsistency and more like careful board positioning, locking pieces in place before the next move.

content:
Trump's announcement to ban institutional investors from buying single family homes is addressing a real problem that mainstream housing debates often ignore or downplay.
Large companies like Invitation Homes, American Homes 4 Rent, and Blackstone are systematically buying single family homes in specific neighborhoods particularly majority Black communities that were devastated by the 2008 foreclosure crisis when families lost everything. 
Once these companies own enough homes in a neighborhood, they control the market.
In some suburban areas around Atlanta and Phoenix, they own up to 78 percent of all rental homes. 
This matters because when these corporate landlords buy homes, the character of entire neighborhoods changes from owner occupied to renter occupied, which fundamentally shifts where wealth goes.​
Think about it this way, when you own a home, you build equity.
Your mortgage payments build your net worth, and eventually you own an asset worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. 
That's how working class families historically built generational wealth. 
But when a corporation owns the home, your rent payments go to shareholders in New York or California, not into your own equity. 
Institutional investors deliberately targeted neighborhoods with economic growth potential, the exact places working families could have climbed the wealth ladder and converted them into rental markets. 
A young family might pay $1,400 per month renting from Invitation Homes or $2,100 per month to own the same home. 
Over 30 years, one path builds wealth, the other enriches a corporation.
The eviction behavior shows how aggressive these companies can be. 
Research found that large corporate landlords in Atlanta filed eviction notices 8 percent more often than small landlords, even after accounting for neighborhood conditions. 
Some private equity firms filed evictions on literally one third of their properties every single year.
 In Atlanta in 2015, 22 percent of all rental households got eviction notices, mostly concentrated in historically Black neighborhoods. 
When you're evicted, you lose your job stability, your kids school stability, your health gets worse and your neighborhood destabilizes.
Institutional investors, under pressure to maximize returns for distant investors, adopted aggressive eviction strategies that destabilized entire communities.​
The targeting was strategic and intentional. 
These companies identified neighborhoods that had recovered from foreclosures (meaning stable), strong population growth (meaning economic opportunity) and weak price to rent ratios (meaning profit potential for them). 
They found working class communities with real economic potential and systematically converted them from owner occupied to rental controlled. 
They didn't build these neighborhoods or pioneer economic growth there, they identified vulnerable communities and extracted wealth from them.​
People who defend institutional investors claim they expand rental supply and operate efficiently, lowering rents. 
That's technically true in some ways, but it completely misses the point. 
Yes, they expanded rentals, but at the cost of homeownership access. 
When institutional investors buy single family homes, the entry level properties where first time buyers typically start and convert them to rentals, they're cutting off the traditional path to wealth building for middle income families earning $25,000–$50,000 annually. 
Those families lose the option to own, instead they're locked into renting to these corporations forever.​
Some argue that banning institutional investors won't solve America's housing shortage, we're short 2 to 4 million housing units due to zoning restrictions that prevent new construction. 
That's true but that's a completely separate problem. 
Just because we need to build more housing doesn't mean we should allow large corporations to monopolize neighborhoods and destabilize communiti[...]
